What is Clean Energy?

Clean energy is power that is produced with little or no air pollution and few greenhouse gas emissions. It comes from sources such as the sun, wind, flowing water, the heat of the Earth, tides, and organic waste, and also from nuclear power. Using it helps protect our health, our climate, and our communities.

Cleaner air and climate

Clean sources release far less carbon dioxide and fewer harmful pollutants than burning coal, oil, or gas.

Often renewable

Many clean sources, like sunlight and wind, are naturally replenished, so they will not run out.

Energy for everyone

SDG 7 aims for affordable, reliable, and modern energy for all people, including remote communities.

Clean energy

  • Very low emissions while generating power
  • Can be produced locally, from resources a country already has
  • Less affected by fuel price swings
  • Supports healthier communities

Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas)

  • Release carbon dioxide and air pollutants when burned
  • Fuel is limited and often imported
  • Prices can rise and fall sharply
  • Linked to air pollution and climate change
Clean is not always the same as renewable. Renewable energy is naturally replenished, like solar and wind. Nuclear power is not renewable, but it is clean because it produces very little carbon pollution while running. Each source has its own benefits and challenges, which you can explore below.

Why It Matters

Why Clean Energy Matters

Clean energy can help reduce air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, improve public health, strengthen energy security, and expand access to reliable electricity. The benefits depend on how each energy source is planned and used, so communities and environmental impacts must be considered.

Healthier communities

Producing electricity with fewer air pollutants can help protect the air people breathe.

More energy choices

Using local resources such as sunshine, wind, and flowing water can diversify how communities get power.

A lower-carbon future

Clean energy can reduce greenhouse gas emissions compared with fossil-fuel electricity.

Energy Sources

Explore Renewable Energy Sources

Renewable energy comes from natural resources that are continuously replenished. Each source works differently, has its own benefits and challenges, and can be used in different ways to meet our energy needs.

Compare all sources

Solar Energy

Solar energy uses sunlight to generate electricity through technologies such as photovoltaic panels. It can be used in homes, schools, businesses, and large-scale solar facilities.

Wind Energy

Wind energy uses the movement of air to turn turbine blades and generate electricity. It can provide renewable power in locations with suitable and consistent wind conditions.

Hydropower

Hydropower uses moving water to generate electricity. It can produce a significant amount of energy, but projects must carefully consider their effects on ecosystems and surrounding communities.

Geothermal Energy

Geothermal energy uses heat from beneath the Earth’s surface to produce useful energy and electricity. It is particularly relevant in the Philippines because of the country’s volcanic and geothermal resources.

Tidal Energy

Tidal energy captures the rise and fall of ocean tides, or the flow of tidal currents, to turn turbines and generate electricity. Tides are predictable, which makes this a reliable renewable source.

Bioenergy

Bioenergy comes from organic materials such as crop residues, animal manure, and food waste. These can be turned into biogas, biofuels, or heat and power for communities.

Nuclear Energy

Nuclear energy uses the heat released by splitting atoms to make steam and generate electricity. It produces very large amounts of low-carbon power around the clock, but requires strict safety and waste management.

Compare the Energy Sources

No energy source is perfect. Each one has strengths, limits, a cost, and an effect on the environment and on people. Use this comparison to see how they stack up. For each source’s full pros and cons, and how it connects to Science, Technology and Society (STS), visit Our Energy Future.

How to read the cost: it is the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), the average cost of producing one kilowatt-hour over a plant’s life, in US dollars. Figures are 2024 global averages for new projects from IRENA, and real costs vary by country and site. IRENA’s figures do not cover nuclear or tidal, so those are described in general terms. See our references.
So which one is best? There is no single winner. Science explains how each source works, technology makes it usable and affordable, and society decides where it goes, who benefits, and who is protected. Most countries combine several sources, based on their resources, their needs, and what their communities choose.
